recent_comments.name: Supramax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: The Supra/Ultra market remained broadly steady over the past few sessions, with activity uneven across regions and sentiment generally cautious. While some isolated fixtures achieved notably strong returns due to vessel positioning and specific requirements, overall trading volumes were relatively limited. The Atlantic showed mixed signals, with firm pockets in some areas but a lack of broad-based momentum. In Asia, activity was affected by holiday in Japan/Far East, although selective opportunities continued to support earnings. Period interest remained stable, reflecting underlying confidence despite a wait-and-see approach from many owners and charterers alike. Overall, the market appears balanced for now, awaiting fresh demand and clearer direction before its next significant move.

recent_comments.name: LNG Market Report
recent_comments.text: After a quiet start to the week, with the market regrouping after a busy Gastech, we now see a surge of firm spot requirements for October laycans particularly in the Atlantic. This renewed demand has started to spur gains in rate expectations, and with several competing cargoes being worked this week, there are encouraging signs of further upward pressure.  Availability does still looks comfortable for first-half October, but pricing through to November is already commanding a sentiment driven premium, given the potential for increased winter production amidst seasonally low storage in Europe and incremental demand in parts of Asia. Portfolios seem likely to hold back tonnage for the time being as these events play out, but we could quickly see a change in the dynamic, with charterers competing for limited flexible open tonnage amidst higher LNG prices heading into winter.  Similarly in the East, on the surface the availability list continues to look extensive. However, since most tonnage is open prompt, the 2H October fixing window is a challenging ask of owners to lock in idle time at prevailing rates just as the market begins to simmer. This is creating some forward scarcity, while fresh demand in the Middle East and cargoes loading out of West Africa also pulling on tonnage adds further competition to Pacific cargoes.  Multi-month and multi-year interest continues, but with the spot market on the turn and Middle East volatility persisting, pricing winter and beyond is becoming increasingly challenging. Whatever the coming weeks bring, it’s unlikely to be dull!

recent_comments.name: Panamax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: The Panamax market has turned this week, with the index reversing the softer trend of the preceding fortnight and all main routes moving higher in unison. The Atlantic has led the recovery: fresh transatlantic enquiry, a steadier flow of NCSA and USG grain stems and a tightening prompt list in the North Continent have allowed owners to hold their ideas, while fronthaul remains the firmer leg and is lending support to shorter intra-basin business. The Pacific is constructive rather than tight – NoPac and Australian coal and grain demand is well distributed and Indonesian volumes have improved, but tonnage remains adequate and owners have found it harder to push materially above last done. The South African and Indian Ocean leg is the swing factor, with that route firming and beginning to compete for the same ships, which should limit downside in the Pacific into the coming weeks. Period interest is active on both Kamsarmax and Panamax with owners quoting to the firmer side of last done, and while bid and offer remain apart, the paper curve carries a modest premium into Q4 and the overall tone into next week is constructive.

recent_comments.name: Aframax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: Rates for local North Sea voyages are reaching record levels and owners are trying to push for a bit more for each cargo being quoted. The tonnage list remains very limited for short voyages, but a bit more candidates for longer voyages. Some owners see ballasting to USG or Mediterranean as good alternatives hence list will continue to look tight for 1st decade October loading dates. Rates in the Mediterranean is also very firm, but feels a bit toppy. However, some voyages give returns over USD 200k pd and as every waiting day is very expensive so owners will look at surrounding markets to minimize waiting adding pressure on tonnage availability. So no expected downside in this market yet.

recent_comments.name: VLCC Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: After last weeks fixing frenzy with rates jumping into the WS 800’s for Fujairah-GOO eastbound cargoes things have calmed down this week. That is not to say that rates are set for a downward spiral, but the immediate upward pressure has eased and some “profit taking” is to be expected. But even if rates were to drop, say 100 points, a WS 700 Fujairah-GOO/East is nevertheless historically highs and if you add 3 zero’s, daily earnings are not far off the WS number. It’s also a logistical challenge to match and load ships at Fujairah to ships coming through the strait of Hormuz and the recent high fixing volume could explain in part why activity has eased as charterers need to clear the decks before adding new ones. However, position lists short term are still tight in both the east and west so players should be warned against a false sense of security in lieu of a perceived activity slowdown.

recent_comments.name: Chartering Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: WEST The positive momentum seen at the end of last week continued into the start of this week, with freight rates moving higher as vessel availability tightened and the arbitrage improved. Mid-October positions were quickly taken up, leaving charterers with fewer options and giving owners greater confidence. Although fixture activity has slowed in recent days, the market remains firm. Relets have gradually been absorbed back into FOB programmes, further reducing the number of available ships for the remaining October cargoes. With tonnage supply continuing to tighten, owners remain in a strong position and freight levels are expected to stay well supported.  EAST In the East, activity remains focused on short-term employment, with continued interest in short-period time charters for STS operations via Sohar and Vadinar. This provides owners with an attractive alternative to the spot market and keeps more vessels in the region. As a result, fewer ships are expected to move West, helping to maintain a tighter tonnage balance.

recent_comments.name: Capesize Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: Capesize markets across the board have seen minor variations but generally very hot on all routes. C3 Brazil/China has seen high rates all week, however quieter activity with slightly flatter rates today as fewer fresh stems came to market ex Brazil and West Africa. C3 Tubarao/China is currently set by Baltic Exchange at USD 43.12. Recently mid October dates have seen offers close to USD 45pmt, with 2H October hovering in the USD 43s and 1H November seeing around USD 43 flat on the offer side. The Pacific markets have seen a flurry of recent fixtures ex West Australia, with early October stems fixing in USD 16.5-16.75 levels. North Atlantic activity has seen a fair amount of fresh interest this week with more fronthaul and transatlantic stems entering the market. Recently offers for transatlantic from Seven Islands to Djen Djen were heard around high USD 24 levels. Earlier in the week a tender was awarded USD 23.75pmt (or USD 52K equivalent) for a Narvik/Erdemir cargo for early October dates. Recent rumors of 60K being done for a transatlantic stem is yet to be confirmed.

recent_comments.name: Suezmax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: A few mysteries have emerged east and west of Suez. The East remains tight on tonnage and rates red hot, whereas in the West supply continues to build. For West Africa supply, we have strong relet presence, a dozen FOC and a dozen to sail over the next 5 days (inclusive of 5 local openers) ETA Nigeria by 15th. In terms of West Africa demand, further tracking suggests there are around 15 cargoes left to move in the 2nd decade. Under normal market conditions, the supply/demand ratio would likely lead to some softening. That said, now more than ever, eastbound voyages are likely to command significant premiums. With the armada already fixed East, those remaining are discouraged from joining the wave, albeit there is always a price. Additionally, there are other forces at play that continue to keep the market interesting and capable of swinging. Aframaxes remain very hot, Sidi barrels are reportedly returning, VLCCs remain extremely tight, and a Trump gasoil export ban will leave Europe yearning for even more crude.

recent_comments.name: SnP Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: With no real end in sight for this relentless tanker bull run, buyers are still willing to pay the ever-increasing price asks from owners. Huge premiums are being paid for prompt tonnage, with good reason, as new owners can expect to write down large portions of the investment over a small number of voyages. For that reason, already cash rich owners will need record levels to part with these immensely profitable assets. Despite plenty of ongoing VLCC negotiations at astronomical levels, the suezmax sector is writing the headlines this week with SPEEDWAY (158k dwt Hyundai 2017) selling for USD 99M.   Activity in the dry sector is extensive this week despite the general firm pricing across the sector. This period could be a prudent time to sell, given the current elevated pricing and the air of uncertainty over rising oil prices and subsequent costs potentially hampering macro demand in 2027. In a usually illiquid market we are seeing new transactions with RTM DIAS/FLINDERS (89K dwt NAMURA 2013) being sold to Chinese buyers for an en bloc price of USD 42.8M.

recent_comments.name: LNG Market Report
recent_comments.text: With Gastech drawing to a close, the rush of fixtures concluded at the tail-end of last week has been followed by a quieter week in fixing terms but a very active few days of meetings and discussions. The ships that have been placed on subjects are at higher levels than we have seen for some weeks, and a broad consensus emerged during Gastech that the market has likely passed through the bottom and will continue to strengthen as we approach the fourth quarter. That said, there was not as much consensus on how far the recovery will take rates or even what would constitute a bullish or bearish winter market. High LNG prices remain and this typically correlates with higher freight and may yet define the winter, but thus far we have seen an inverse relationship as owners and sub-letters have fixed lower rates to mitigate the higher boil-off costs of idling. While this dynamic remains and as LNG prices push higher, it is likely to act as a ceiling on freight until (or unless) traders and portfolios begin pulling tonnage back into their own fleets.   Thank you to all our friends, old and new, who helped to make Bangkok such a successful gathering, and for those travelling back in the coming days: safe travels!

recent_comments.name: Chartering Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: VLGC freight ex US back at all-time high levels with several deals subfixed at $300+ HCvP so far this week. Last done is currently at $325 HCvP on a Neo Panama vessel which brings the fixture count for October to 25 spot deals (5/12/8 by decade). There are currently only a handful of vessels available for spot enquiries during last decade October and it is worth noting that the market is 10 fixtures short of the YTD average on a monthly basis (35).  While we still see several uncovered requirements ex US in October, some players have already surfaced for 1st decade November cargos as freight remains very tight.

recent_comments.name: Suezmax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: Split Stems ex BRZ & West Africa along with an influx of USG/EAST serves to populate the Atlantic basin heavily with enquiry. Rates, whilst astronomical, did not price in the huge demand upside this market had & still has amidst an dearth of VLCCs. VLCC availability for Brazil upto end October could be as low as 4-5 ships incl projections and with USG/West Africa markets drawing down on the same pool that leaves collossal volumes for Suezmaxes. 36MBBLS ex West Africa alone are outstanding upto 20th October, vs 38 logical ships either FOC, ex local positions or ETS within 7 days. Again these must be portioned across both sides of the Atlantic.  CPC has failed to keep pace. In fact the recent fixtures at 500 level are more an indication that some owners, in spite of market momentum, are prioritising minimising waiting time to optimise TCEs. This is characteristic of the market in general and, along with the tonnage taken on Short TC cheaper than market TCEs, has stopped the market in general from roofing for now. Rather than fixing forward as usual, CPC, partially due to a delay in stem releases is working prompter than the Atlantic basin, but once it shifts to 8-10 onwards the expectation is that TD6 ticks up.  Meanwhile the MEG, bolstered by VLCC rates, has climbed to 130x690 levels FUJA/EAST - there are availabilities east of suez, but a good amount of these won't go near the region, instead they are set to head to COGH. Given the severely limited availability on VLCC solid demand is expected here also.

recent_comments.name: VLCC Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: VLCC rates for a Fuj/East run are now 3/4 on the way to WS 1000! Arguably charterers and trades alike also have themselves to “blame” as they have relet ships at increased intervals as well. The Atlantic market is also firing on all cylinders although mainly left for Suezmaxes now as VLCC supply is running out. All in all access to physical crude trumps freights at the moment as refineries are scrambling for supply. The big concern ‌is ⁠the disruption to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and Yanbu export infrastructure, following attacks on Saudi energy facilities. Saudi Arabia is reportedly now offering more loadings of crude oil to Asian refiners via ship-to-ship transfers off Oman's Sohar port. However, visible vessel transits through the Strait of Hormuz remain in the single digits.

recent_comments.name: Aframax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: NSEA A less populated list, firm surrounding markets and Charterers reaching further out has all pushed the NSea up pushing close to 100 ws points  since the middle of last week.  Natural working window is now pushing towards 28-29 dates.  The first 5 days of October stems are relatively balanced month on month but we should start to see natural tonnage come back around heading into October. Market remains firm for the time being it seems. MED TCE remains massive in all markets across the West with the Mediterranean market still busy despite the withdrawal of all STS Port Said/Sidi cargoes. Ceyhan dates have pushed to end-month now while Libya is still around mid-3rd decade. The list is balanced and won't replenish too much before 22-23sep and West Med positions could  give priority to the USG market.

recent_comments.name: Capesize Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: This week we saw softening sentiment across the Capesize basins. Today activity across Atlantic and Pacific was fairly quiet following last week's market highs; sentiment turned negative as we saw C3 and C5 easing yesterday. Pacific weakness dominated as yesterday's fixtures concluded in the mid USD 16s, well below the earlier week USD 17+ offers, reflecting a lack of bidding in the pacific. This morning a recent fixture reported for a West Australian fixture at USD 15.95 for early October laycans, signaling potential further softening. Atlantic sentiment also flattened with TA and FH under pressure as forward offers struggle to find support. Although todays C3 index rose slightly to USD 42.46, owners continue to offer at mid USD 43 levels with little feedback, and yesterday we saw last done levels for mid-October dates around mid-low USD 42. Both basins overall have seen a loss in momentum compared to last week's hot market. FFAs has mixed sentiment with future freight showing slight upside going forward.

recent_comments.name: Supramax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: The Supramax market saw mixed sentiment, with softer conditions in North America offset by improving levels in the East, particularly on backhauls. The Continent also showed signs of improvement, although reported activity remained limited. ECSA remained active, while the Indian Ocean continued to see healthy demand with little change in levels. Improved sentiment in Asia brought renewed period interest, with owners showing greater confidence. Overall, the market continued its upward trend, supported by stronger Eastern sentiment and steady activity across several regions.  The Handy market remained relatively quiet, with limited fresh information but a generally healthy underlying tone. The Continent and Mediterranean stayed broadly balanced, with rates holding steady. The South Atlantic and USG continued to show firmer sentiment, supported by healthy demand and tightening prompt tonnage. Asia remained subdued, although sufficient cargo volumes helped keep the market broadly stable. Overall, the market was steady to slightly firmer, with regional variations in momentum.

recent_comments.name: Panamax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: The Panamax market has drifted lower through the week, with the softer tone now evident across both basins. In the Atlantic, a steady build of prompt tonnage in the North Continent, together with a lengthening list of ballasters arriving into ECSA, has shifted the balance in charterers' favour; fronthaul has proved more resilient on the back of continued US-origin grain and coal demand, but TA business has borne the brunt of the correction. The Pacific, which had outperformed into early September, has likewise lost momentum, with charterers stepping back and bidding conservatively – NoPac grain rounds and a steady flow of Australian and Indo coal are providing a floor rather than a driver. Period interest remains genuine, with charterers engaged on one- and two-year cover, but owners' ideas and charterers' bids have yet to converge, and modest backwardation beyond the fourth quarter is tempering appetite at the top end. Our read into next week is cautious: absent a fresh wave of cargo replenishment in the Atlantic, we expect a sideways-to-softer tone, with any recovery more likely to originate in the Pacific.

recent_comments.name: SnP Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: The tanker market bonanza continues this week with earnings on large crude tonnage consistently beating last done, sending asset values even further upwards. There is a scramble for prompt ships east of Suez, with willing sellers continuing to set ever higher benchmarks . ONEX have emerged as the latest buyer in this space, being linked to a number of transactions this week, details on which units will likely be uncovered in the coming weeks. Another buyer, KPC, have been reported purchasing scrubber fitted VLCC KALLISTA (317k dwt Hyundai 2010) for a sensational USD 130M. Elsewhere, Hercules picked up LR1 pair MARLIN HESTIA/HERA (74k dwt Sungdong 2017) for USD 49M apiece.   The dry space has been somewhat in the shadow of the tanker market but in continuation of the theme of late, impressive figures are being paid for available units. Owners may consider now a good time to sell, given some uncertainty on the horizon in 2027 from a global geopolitical and meteorological standpoint, as well as anticipated fleet growth. This week GESCO are reported to have bought scrubber fitted BW JAPAN (81k dwt Tsuneishi 2019) at USD 38.5M.

recent_comments.name: LNG Market Report
recent_comments.text: The market has seen an increase in chartering activity across the basins, and this coupled with stronger delivered gas prices has provided some support to sentiment if not yet to rates. Attention is now shifting towards the October fixing window, a time when the market is typically firming rapidly. It is therefore unsurprising that some players seek to capitalize on the persistently weak market conditions to build winter coverage at levels that remain well below those seen earlier in the year. TFDE vessels have continued to face challenges in the spot market, struggling to compete on a UFC basis even for smaller cargo parcels, in part because of the prevalence of 2-stroke availability shown by portfolios.  There are some promising signs for the optimist to point to, including the recent transit of a laden LNGC from Qatar to Pakistan (and signs other Qatari vessels are ballasting towards the Gulf) and a likely uptick in vessels repositioning themselves back to the Atlantic for what lies in store during the Winter season. The outcome of the firm requirements being worked today may shed some light on whether the positive sentiment building will translate into significant rate gains despite the oversupply on fundamentals.

recent_comments.name: Capesize Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: This week on Capesize, we saw continued resilience in both Pacific and Atlantic basins as market levels held strong at peak levels. C5 West Australia/Qingdao saw a paper peaked on Friday as the Baltic printed USD 18.96. Today levels are climbing after a slight dip early week as the Pacific market sees robust activity with latest offers in the low USD 19s. A flurry of recent fixtures reported in the USD 18.4-18.5 region for late September and early October laycans and one rumor suggests that a very recent fixture was seen in the low USD 19 levels, but this is unconfirmed. In the Atlantic, C3 Brazil/China led the charge as owners remained bullish, holding firm on offers. A tight tonnage has owners staying strong with their offers, today seeing numerous offers in the USD mid 42-43 levels for late 2h October laycans. Bids for late October sit at high USD 41s with one fixture seen last night at high USD 41 levels, and another Newcastlemax took an early October cargo for USD 41. Sentiment is mixed moving forward as FFAs signal slight flattening overall, owners remain bullish, holding firm on their offers, operators are quietly watching the market suggesting potential upside risk if demand persists at current levels.

recent_comments.name: Chartering Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: The week has been quiet, with events and travel on the agenda for many in the market, and only one fixture reported. While tensions in the Middle East are rising again, in the West the Panama Canal remains a problem, meaning LOTSA slots, Panamaxes and higher-ranking booking codes are increasingly important for secure passage. Cape-only options are also becoming more common as many avoid the passage risk altogether, and recently we have seen a convergence in routing, with Cape and Panama ballasting options now close to equal.   The position list still shows two ships for September dates. October carries 12 ships, split three, eight and one across the three decades. Fixing activity remains limited, but ideas vary between USD 265 and 275 for October dates. So far we have seen 11 fixtures for October, while September fixtures tally 33 to date, just three shy of August.

recent_comments.name: Panamax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: After several weeks of steady gains the Panamax market has levelled off, with the index easing gently over recent sessions from what now looks to have been an early-September high. The Atlantic accounts for most of the softening: prompt tonnage has built up in the North Continent while fresh transatlantic enquiry has slowed, leaving owners there with less leverage, though fronthaul remains the firmer part of the basin and owners continue to favour Atlantic employment over repositioning east. The Pacific has held its ground more comfortably, supported by Australian and Indonesian coal, North Pacific grain and a useful flow of additional cargo from split Capesize stems, but the urgency that characterised late August has faded and charterers are no longer chasing. Period remains active and, notably, better bid than the softening spot market would imply – business is still clearing at levels close to recent highs, with owners of modern tonnage holding their ideas firmly and the gap to charterers' bids widening rather than closing. Our own indicators argue for caution from here: shipment volumes continue to run below fleet supply growth, the South Atlantic tightness reading suggests the recent correction has further to run, and we would treat the current period market as an opportunity to secure cover rather than expect a renewed push higher.

recent_comments.name: Supramax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: The Handy market remained stable, and even firmed up a touch, with a healthy balance between supply and demand. Activity was mainly focused on spot and short-period employment, with owners generally able to remain selective. Touch positive bias, provided grain programs and other minor bulk cargoes continue at current levels. Balanced tonnage availability should, however, keep freight gains measured.  The Supramax/Ultramax market showed a slightly firmer tone during the week, supported by improving activity in the Atlantic and steady demand in the Pacific. Owners remained selective, while charterers continued to show some resistance on rates. Overall sentiment is constructive but balanced. Recent gains suggest some tightening in the Atlantic, while adequate tonnage availability in Asia is limiting stronger upside.

recent_comments.name: Suezmax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: * The majority of the publicly reported WAF cargoes have either fixed away or may have relets to utilise. As a result, we are likely pushing into the 27-30 September fixing window.  * However, despite this shift towards fixing closer to three weeks forward, there is little expectation that activity will slow, with adjacent sizes either already pulling their weight or primed to do so.  * Aframaxes are surging in the Med and, if the physical/paper dynamic is anything to go by, are expected to do the same stateside.  * In addition, and perhaps more significantly, the VLCC market is extremely busy ex-Fujairah and approaching our equivalent with the Atlantic also firming aggressively.  * Regardless of pricing, VLCCs remain under-fixed for the first decade of October ex-WAF, and with this surge in Eastern activity there may be very few units physically capable of interacting with this window, which could inevitably lead to cargo splitting and increased Suezmax utilisation. * To top it all off, CPC stems should be released imminently, and there are reports of attacks on terminal infrastructure and vessels, which will almost certainly result in higher premiums.

recent_comments.name: VLCC Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: The VLCC positions list is now so tight that no one would be too surprised if we see the W400 mark breached for a Fujairah/east for a prompt-ish position before the week is over, crazy as it may sound. Speed blindness does not even begin to describe the current mood. However, the oil still needs to get out through the Strait of Hormuz and Iranians have increased efforts to stop that from happening. It’s a fragile state of affairs. Atlantic/east rates have followed suit as refiners look for supply security regardless of higher oil prices. Ship values have also skyrocketed in tandem with the spot market with reports of new building resales at $200 million- and 16–17-year-olds more than half of that. Fasten seat belts.

recent_comments.name: Aframax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: As North Sea Aframax loading dates are now moving into the third decade of September, the list of available tonnage continues to thin. With neighbouring markets such as the US Gulf and Mediterranean offering attractive alternatives, owners are increasingly ballasting away from the North Sea. While rates remain steady for the time being, tightening tonnage availability could support a modest upward correction in the near term. Activity in the Mediterranean remains robust, with cargoes being quoted from virtually every export area and loading port. Rates continue to gain momentum, and with charterers actively seeking to secure tonnage for forward-loading programmes, the market is expected to remain firm with further upside potential.

recent_comments.name: SnP Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: Further flare ups in the USA-Iran conflict this week have only added to the disruption in the tanker market. This will help to sustain the current high earnings and valuations environment, and with no solution in sight, it is fair to say levels on both are likely to increase in the near term. While other modern units remain under discussion in the MR space, 12-year-old unit LVM AARON (50k dwt Dae Sun 2014) was the only sale in this subsector, selling to Besiktas for USD 35.5M. Elsewhere, Greek buyers are reported to have purchased scrubber fitted CABO SAN VINCENTE (63k dwt STX 2008)*Ice 1A for USD 22M.   Capesize bulkers are leading the way for dry tonnage, breaking through the USD 50k/day threshold on the spot market. Would-be sellers of capes are now likely to think twice before committing ships unless buyers can beat last done, given the bumper earnings are also bleeding into term rates. Such is displayed by scrubber fitted CAPE CONDOR (180k dwt Koyo 2010) selling this week for USD 39M, mere days after scrubber fitted ERATO (180k dwt Imabari 2010) was sold for USD 38M. Asset pricing across all sizes on dry remains firm, however there appears to be no shortage of buyers given the earnings on offer.

recent_comments.name: Chartering Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: Inefficiencies in various parts of the shipping world continues to keep freight on a tight leash.  The strength is coming from a strong arb, tight shipping availability driven by Panama Canal restrictions and subsequently with both ballast and laden legs increasingly routed via Cape. TS Edouard's impact is reportedly limited to the Sabine Pass.  With August loadings complete, routing shows roughly 30 of 110 departures via Cape to discharge East, against Panama Canal auction fee levels and transit uncertainty.  Whilst there are only a couple September vessels left, fixing activity pivots to October. The October position list now shows 2 first-decade, 7 second-decade, 1 third-decade. In other words, very tight availability for spot shipping.

recent_comments.name: Container Activity
recent_comments.text: Strong

recent_comments.name: Aframax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: North Sea After a long weekend activity has been slow on the pick up. Natural dates 8-10 window but with a number of relets around and stems a little thin charterers are able to take their time. US market looks to have bottomed and with Mediterranean market looking softer we may see drive to ballast towards the US again after a quiet few days on that front. Slow but steady.  Mediterranean Activity stalled at the end of last week which has rebuilt the early part of the list. Activity has picked up again at the start of the week but the increased tonnage has changed the sentiment for now and charterers have managed to pushed the market down. Natural window pushing into the 2nd decade with tonnage to clear which in the short term may lead to some more weakening before we find the bottom.

recent_comments.name: LNG Market Report
recent_comments.text: Summer holidays in Europe are over and chartering activity has returned, with September laycans in the U.S. largely covered now and the gaze raising to October. Surplus vessels remain but as enquiries begin to build, there has been renewed interest for periods covering winter. Rate expectations are a significant discounts to average traded levels for modern vessels for this time of year, and reflect the growing sense that weak shipping fundamentals will override high LNG pricing and trading opportunities. Whether the Winter bid continues to improve remains to be seen, but a bridging of the wide bid/offer spread suggests a softer view of winter and that portfolios continue to edge to the long side heading into a Q4 where Qatari supply is still stranded and DES markets East and West keep putting off demand until it really hits. The Pacific has now corrected with challenging supply/demand balance, and unfortunately for owners the market has come off rather than the Atlantic market picking up. The few multi-month fixtures reported suggest that several players see this as the bottom of the market – so perhaps rates can only strengthen from here?

recent_comments.name: Supramax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: The Supramax market remained mixed and largely directionless, with activity picking up selectively across both the Atlantic and Asia. The Atlantic saw pockets of strength, particularly around the USG and South Atlantic, supported by steady demand for grains, petcoke and minor bulks, while Asia remained active but positional with varied tonnage availability between areas. Handysize trading was generally subdued, although fundamentals remained healthy in parts of the Pacific and South Atlantic. The US Gulf continued to show relatively firm conditions despite limited fixing, while the Continent and Mediterranean markets remained softer. Overall, sentiment across both sectors remains cautious, with regional tonnage positioning and pockets of enquiry driving the market rather than any clear broader trend. There is good appetite for period with quite a few fixtures reported past weeks.

recent_comments.name: Capesize Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: Capesize is heating up across all segments, with both C3 and C5 trade routes posting some of the highest numbers seen this year. Last done on C3 Brazil/China today was seen at USD 40.9, setting a new benchmark which hasn't been seen since the peak of 2021. FFAs are up for the coming quarter, Baltic C3 prints USD 40.2 today and C5 is also showing strong activity with last done in the mid USD 16s and rumors of a fixture at USD 17 flat (yet to be confirmed). C5 West Australia/China prints USD 16.5 today on the Baltic, jumping 7.59% today, overtaking C3 Brazil/China as the higher earner per day between C3 and C5. With an uptick of ballasters headed for Brazil toward the end of September, we may see some pressure in the Atlantic for late September and early October laycans. Overall sentiment is bullish but cautious as limited fresh demand to absorb growing supply.

recent_comments.name: Suezmax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: Despite Suezmaxes regaining competitiveness against VLCCs following last week’s sharp correction, a front-heavy tonnage list and muted activity have continued to weigh on the rates in West Africa. Meanwhile, Aframaxes remain firmly in the driving seat across the Atlantic. That said, the improved economics of the Suezmaxes appear to be attracting renewed interest, with activity showing signs of picking up.

recent_comments.name: Panamax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: The Panamax market has firmed steadily through the week, with the gains broadening across both basins as the index pushed higher over successive sessions. In the Atlantic the tone is constructive: transatlantic business remains well bid on the back of a replenished cargo book and a tightening nearby tonnage list, while fronthaul has been slower to follow, with owners holding above charterers' ideas on US Gulf and South American grain. The Pacific has been the stronger of the two, where a steady flow of Australian and Indonesian coal alongside North Pacific grain has left prompt tonnage short and charterers chasing owners' levels rather than the reverse. Period interest has picked up markedly, with a good spread of owners collecting for both short and twelve-month cover and bids increasingly obliged to follow last-done rather than set it, although the forward curve continues to price modest backwardation beyond the prompt. We expect the tone to remain sideways-to-firmer into next week, with the main question being how much of the recent move reflects genuine incremental demand rather than positioning ahead of the autumn grain programme.

recent_comments.name: VLCC Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: The situation in the Strait of Hormuz is becoming more precarious by the hour as the US-Iran conflict has intensified again. Several tankers have been hit, and reports suggest that a fully laden VLCC has been abandoned by its crew. The possibility of a major oil spill would of course be a natural disaster but will also bring more focus on the condition of ships which do make it through and their safety when it comes to performing ship to ship operations. A number of discounted Somo tenders never made it through the strait resulting in some failures of fixtures done in the last couple of days at inflated rates. With that some of the immediate pressure has eased slightly, but the position list still remains wanting and rates are unlikely to go much down any time soon. The Atlantic position list is even more challenging, and the likes of oil major Petrobras reportedly only had 1 offer yesterday for a Brazil/China enquiry by the deadline, on and ex d/d ship which wasn’t workable. There’s also reports of another Brazilian export cargo working off the market. Add to that a couple of charterers sniffing ex West Africa and a tender or two USG/Eastbound and it’s a perfect “storm”. Arguably the Suezmax market has seen a drop lately and will eventually cap the upside for their bigger sisters.

recent_comments.name: SnP Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: Record profits in the crude space continue to fuel rampant tanker buying appetite. Lofty valuations, even for this market, are being met by buyers who are targeting prompt tonnage, often bypassing usual concerns such as yard or survey dates. The suezmax sector has seen particular action this week with new benchmarks being set across the curve. Scrubber fitted CAPE BENAT (156k dwt Rongsheng 2010) sold at USD 62.5M to Lila Global, and SS due ANTIGUA I (157k dwt New Times 2016) sold for USD 90M.    The dry bulk market action is more modest by comparison, but still healthy for this time of year. Owners are in a luxurious position of having the option to sell ageing tonnage at firm valuations, or indeed just keep operating their ships in healthy earnings environments. The supramax sector was busiest this week with a flurry of transactions, helping to price the older end of the curve. With the Q4 supra/ultra futures curve sitting around the USD 20K/day mark, buyers are clearly plentiful. The 20-year-old benchmark was set with SPAR SCORPIO (53k dwt Chengxi 2006) sold for USD 11.5M despite surveys being due in October of this year.

recent_comments.name: Chartering Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: The September list is down to 10 vessels, and October dates are starting to come into view. Panama NB/SB fees remain a real dissuader, and it's showing up in the routing split: ballasters from Asia are now going 50/50 Cape versus Panama, up from roughly 25% back in June and July. Fixture activity has been quiet this week, just a handful done, with owners' ideas mid/low USD 260's.

recent_comments.name: LNG Activity
recent_comments.text: Slow

recent_comments.name: Supramax Weekly Comment
recent_comments.text: The Supramax market remained largely subdued and stable. The Atlantic was mixed, with the Mediterranean gradually softening while the Continent saw some fresh enquiry and the US Gulf and South Atlantic remained broadly balanced. In the Pacific, activity was stronger in the NOPAC and parts of Southeast Asia, while Indonesian coal activity was relatively limited. The Handysize market showed a modestly firmer tone, supported by improving cargos in East Coast South America, tighter prompt tonnage in parts of the Pacific and better sentiment in the US Gulf. While the US Gulf was still soft in the short term despite expectations of improvement ahead.
